  "question": "Can I launch one lending market first and expand it later to support more assets?",
  "short_answer": "Yes. Launching a single lending market first and adding assets later is a common and sound approach in DeFi. Whether it is easy depends on how the protocol is architected, especially whether new markets can be added without redeploying core contracts and migrating user funds.",
  "why_it_works": [
    "Each asset market has its own risk parameters (collateral factors, liquidation thresholds, interest rate model, oracle, supply and borrow caps), so a market can be validated on its own before others are added.",
    "A narrow launch limits smart contract audit scope, oracle dependencies, and the number of liquidity and bad-debt risks you must monitor at go-live."
  ],
  "architecture_options": [
    {
      "model": "Per-asset deployments",
      "description": "Deploy a separate market contract for each base asset. Compound v3 (Comet) uses this pattern, with separate markets such as the USDC and WETH base-asset markets.",
      "pros": "Simple to reason about and easy to launch one at a time.",
      "cons": "Liquidity stays fragmented across markets, and each new deployment repeats operational and audit work."
    },
    {
      "model": "Singleton with permissionless market creation",
      "description": "A single core contract holds many isolated markets, each defined by loan token, collateral token, oracle, interest rate model, and LLTV. Morpho Blue follows this pattern.",
      "pros": "New markets can be added without touching core contracts, and the core is audited once.",
      "cons": "Market creation must be gated or curated carefully, and bad markets can still hurt their own lenders and borrowers."
    },
    {
      "model": "Shared pool with isolation or siloed assets",
      "description": "Aave v3 supports adding reserves to a shared pool, along with isolation mode and e-mode for risk control. Silo Finance isolates each asset pair into its own silo.",
      "pros": "Aave v3 benefits from deep shared liquidity, while Silo's isolation limits contagion.",
      "cons": "Adding reserves to a shared pool is a governance-heavy process with its own risk review."
    },
    {
      "model": "Vault-based modular lending",
      "description": "Euler v2 uses modular vaults and an EVK-style framework where markets are composed from reusable components.",
      "pros": "Flexible expansion and composability.",
      "cons": "More architectural complexity to design and audit."
    }
  ],
  "recommendations": [
    "Design the first market as an instance of a reusable market template or factory, so the second asset is a configuration change rather than a new codebase.",
    "Keep oracle, interest rate model, and risk parameters configurable per market, and do not hardcode a single asset.",
    "Plan the governance or admin path for adding markets up front, including who can list assets, how caps are set, and how emergency pausing works per market.",
    "Avoid migrating user funds when expanding. Adding markets alongside the first one is far less risky than replacing it.",
    "Decide early between isolated markets (safer, fragmented liquidity) and shared liquidity (deeper liquidity, more contagion risk), since changing this later is hard.",
    "Budget audits for each new asset's integration (oracle and token behavior, such as fee-on-transfer or rebasing tokens) rather than assuming the core audit covers it."

    "Each asset market has its own risk parameters (collateral factors, liquidation thresholds, interest rate model, oracle, supply and borrow caps), so a market can be validated on its own before others are added.",

      "cons": "Liquidity stays fragmented across markets, and each new deployment repeats operational and audit work."

      "model": "Singleton with permissionless market creation",
      "description": "A single core contract holds many isolated markets, each defined by loan token, collateral token, oracle, interest rate model, and LLTV. Morpho Blue follows this pattern.",
